Yesterday I had a little bit of fun. But as I was progressing to find a kind of likeness of primality for "very" strong pseudo prime, my OpenAI conversation was deleted. So I became a little bit paranoid, so I just wanted to share my results before seing them elsewhere and ask a Lean opinion in the same time.

I was looking at composite numbers that pass several strong probable prime tests, including Miller–Rabin tests with small bases and Lucas type probable prime tests. I made severals test but the best results was the combinaison I tested composites with base 2, base 3 and base 5, and I kept only the numbers that passed all three tests even though they were not prime.

Then I compared those surviving composites using Euler's totient function.

For a prime p

φ(p) = p - 1

so I defined

R(n) = φ(n) / (n - 1)

The closer R(n) is to 1, the closer the totient of n is to the exact prime case. My goal here was to create a ratio to compare strong pseudoprimes with each other according to how close their Euler totient is to the prime case.

Among the numbers I compared, the best value I found was

57 296 609 361 082 111

with factorization 207297991 × 276397321

Euler's totient gives

φ(n) = 57 296 608 877 386 800

so n has exactly 57 296 608 877 386 800 positive integers below it that are coprime to it, and only 483 695 310 that are not coprime to it.

This gives

R(n) = φ(n) / (n - 1) = 99.9999991558046 percent

The next two highest values I found were

56560510115046901 with R(n) = 99.9999991417028 percent

56459192044371901 with R(n) = 99.9999991409330 percent

Then I compared this result with other metrics, including Riemann based prime counting approximations, inverse prime counting estimates, Axler based estimates, and prime gap centering. Among the 20 values I tested, only 57296609361082111 ranked first both with my ratio R(n) and with the prime-gap centering method.

Can the ratio φ(n)/(n - 1) be formalized in Lean as a measure that ranks composite numbers by their totient proximity to the prime case? Would it be usefull?
